Annual Meetings

Afternoon Session - 2006 Meeting

Warren Buffett supports a path to citizenship for people in the U.S. illegally, tells investors why they shouldn't let markets "instruct" them, and concedes that after many years of criticism, business schools are actually getting better.

Sat, May 6 2006 • 1:00 PM EDT
Key Chapters —
  1. 1. Buffett favors path to citizenship for some illegal immigrants
  2. 2. Business schools have improved "considerably"
  3. 11. We love reading them, but newspapers are in trouble
  4. 12. Don't let your fear overcome your logic
  5. 23. Key distinction between insurance and gambling

Sync Video to Paragraph

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah. Well, Ben Graham said long ago that you're neither right nor wrong because people agree with you or disagree with you.

Sync Video to Paragraph

In other words, being contrarian has no special virtue over being a trend follower.

Sync Video to Paragraph

You're right because your facts and reasoning are right. So all you do is you try to make sure that the facts you have are correct. And that's usually pretty easy to do in this country. I mean, information is available on all kinds of things. Internet makes it even easier.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And then once you have the facts, you've got to think through what they mean. And you don't take a public opinion survey. You don't pay attention to things that are unimportant. I mean, what you're looking for is something â things that are important and knowable.

Sync Video to Paragraph

If something's important but unknowable, forget it. I mean, it may be important, you know, whether somebody's going to drop a nuclear weapon tomorrow but it's unknowable. It may be all kinds of things. So you â and there are all kinds of things are that knowable but are unimportant.

Sync Video to Paragraph

In focusing on business and investment decisions, you try to think â you narrow it down to the things that are knowable and important, and then you decide whether you have information of sufficient value that â you know, compared to price and all that â that will cause you to act.

Sync Video to Paragraph

What others are doing means nothing. It's what Graham writes in Chapter 8 of "The Intelligent Investor," that the market is there to serve you and not to instruct you. That's of enormous importance.

Sync Video to Paragraph

When people talk about momentum in stocks or charting or any kind of things like that, they're saying that the market is instructing you. The market doesn't instruct us; the market is there to serve us.

Sync Video to Paragraph

If it does something silly, we get a chance to do something because it's doing something silly. We do it. But it doesn't tell us anything. It just tells us prices.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And if the price is out of line where the facts and reasoning lead you, then you â then action is called for. And if it doesn't, you forget it and go play bridge that day and the next day, see whether there's something new. And the nice thing is there always is something new.

Sync Video to Paragraph

I mentioned the LTCM crisis. We were getting calls on Sunday from people that had portfolios that were in trouble. Now, I will tell you that if â you can make a lot of money on Sunday.

Sync Video to Paragraph

You may not get a chance very often, but any calls you get on Sunday you're probably going to make money on. (Laughter)

Sync Video to Paragraph

Things are really screwed up if you're getting calls on Sunday. And all you have to do is make sure that you're the callee and not the caller â (laughs) on Sunday.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But if you get those calls â you get a call on a Sunday and somebody says that the off-the-run is trading 30 basis points away from the on-the-run, you know, all you have to do is decide whether â how you handle that particular piece of information â whether it's correct in the first place â but how you handle that piece of information, whether you can play out your hand.
